title: Gradiant Wins Five India Contracts as Chip Boom Turns on Water
excerpt: The Boston water-technology company named a new India chief and will expand its Indian workforce by more than 40 percent as it supplies ultrapure water and zero-liquid-discharge systems to semiconductor, circuit-board and solar factories.
body:
• Gradiant won five new design-build water contracts across semiconductor, printed-circuit-board and solar manufacturing in India, including a repeat award from a global chipmaker expanding its fab.
  • The company named Hari Prasad, a water-industry veteran of nearly 30 years, as Managing Director, India, and plans to grow its India team by more than 40% this year.
  • Gradiant says its India orders are on track to more than double this year, with revenue set to more than triple, driven by demand for ultrapure water and zero-liquid-discharge compliance.
  • The push mirrors a $300 million semiconductor-water contract haul in the United States this year, underscoring how water has become a strategic constraint on the AI supply chain.

Water has quietly become one of the most expensive ingredients in the chips that power artificial intelligence, and Gradiant is betting that India will be its next big market. The Boston-based water-technology company announced on Tuesday a series of India milestones: five new design-build contracts across semiconductor, printed circuit board and solar manufacturing, a new Managing Director for the country, and plans to grow its India team by more than 40% this year.

The contracts, according to the company's announcement in Chennai, cover ultrapure water, wastewater treatment and zero liquid discharge (ZLD) systems. They include a repeat award from a global chipmaker that is expanding its fabrication plant and came back to Gradiant for the next phase. Gradiant said customers chose it for high water recovery, reliable ZLD performance and speed of execution.

Why water is the new power for chipmaking

A modern chip fab consumes tens of millions of litres of water a day. Silicon wafers must be washed in ultrapure water far cleaner than drinking water at dozens of steps in the manufacturing process, and the wastewater that comes back out carries hydrofluoric acid and other chemicals that regulators do not allow into rivers or groundwater. In India, where several states mandate zero liquid discharge for industrial units, fabs and solar plants have to recycle nearly everything they use.

That makes water availability, reliability and ZLD compliance as strategic as power and land in deciding where, and how fast, manufacturing capacity gets built, Gradiant said. The company styles itself "the water layer of the AI economy," delivering everything from ultrapure water production to high-recovery wastewater treatment and scrubber reclaim as a single accountable partner.

India's factory bet, and the engineering behind it

Gradiant named Hari Prasad as Managing Director, India, to lead growth across semiconductors, data centers and energy. Prasad brings nearly 30 years of water-technology leadership, most recently as General Manager of Industrial Water at Pentair, following senior roles across India, the Middle East and Africa.

"India is fast becoming one of the most important places to build the AI supply chain, from chips to circuit boards to solar cells," said Prakash Govindan, Gradiant's chief executive. "When a chipmaker comes back to us for its next expansion, that is the strongest endorsement we can get."

"A fab or a solar plant can't run a single shift without water, and the ZLD rules here leave no room for shortcuts. That is exactly where Gradiant wins."

— Hari Prasad, Managing Director, Gradiant India

The company is expanding its India team across engineering, project execution, operations and digital roles, including at its Engineering Center in Coimbatore, which supports Gradiant projects worldwide. Prasad said the company's India orders are on track to more than double this year, with revenue set to more than triple.

What it means for India's chip ambitions

The five contracts land as India tries to convert semiconductor announcements into operating factories. Policy tailwinds under the India Semiconductor Mission have drawn fab and assembly proposals from Tata, CG Power, Micron and others, but each project ultimately stands or falls on execution details like water, power and waste handling — the unglamorous infrastructure that determines whether a plant runs at full utilization.

Gradiant's pitch is that water is the tightest of those constraints. Its September announcement of $300 million in new US semiconductor contracts — spanning five fabrication sites in New York, Virginia, Idaho and Utah — suggests chipmakers on both sides of the world now treat water as a first-order supply-chain risk, not an afterthought. The company, valued at about $2 billion according to the Phoenix Business Journal, is targeting a $1 billion US order book next year.

The diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in technology, the story is a small window into how India's chip story gets built: not in boardroom announcements but in engineering centers like the one in Coimbatore, whose teams design water systems for projects around the world. Gradiant's India expansion adds to a growing cluster of deep-tech roles — water process engineers, digital specialists, project managers — that sit at the intersection of India's manufacturing ambitions and global clean-tech careers.

What's next

Watch for Gradiant to name the customers behind the five contracts and for hiring to accelerate in Coimbatore. The larger question is whether India's first wave of fabs can meet their water and ZLD obligations at the pace the projects demand. If the company's bet pays off, the quiet business of cleaning fab wastewater could become one of the most reliable barometers of India's semiconductor build-out.
